title: Technical feasibility, sustainability and technoeconomic analysis of non-wood fibre integration in paper-based flexible packaging: a case study of India
content: The environmental persistence of flexible plastics has driven a shift towards the development of paper-based alternatives. Integrating non-wood fibres into paper production is receiving increasing interest due to perceived environmental benefits and cost reduction compared to papers produced from virgin wood sources. This study investigates how integrating non-wood fibres impacts the physical properties, production costs and environmental impacts of paper produced in India, which represents a market with high volumes of products sold in flexible packaging. Papers in India are largely produced from combinations of softwood and hardwood pulps with a high dependence on softwood imports. Bagasse, bamboo and old corrugated cardboard were utilised to substitute 20% of virgin wood fibres; softwood, hardwood or both. Paper hand sheets were produced using TAPPI T205 sp-02 and key performance indicators including tensile index, porosity, air permeability and surface roughness, were characterised. Substituting imported softwood with locally-sourced non-wood fibres relates to a production cost of $761–$770 USD per ton and a global warming potential (GWP) between 1.88 and 1.93 kg CO2 eq. per kg paper, representing an 11–12% reduction in cost and 27–29% reduction in GWP compared to the virgin wood fibre benchmark. Cost and GWP savings are driven by reduced transport impacts to import the softwood and establishing more localised supply chains. Non-wood fibre inclusion generally maintains or improves the physical properties of papers, compared to the virgin wood benchmark. Hand sheets produced using bagasse as a substitute for softwood displayed a tensile index of 28.9 N m g−1 and a Gurley time of 1.0 s/10 mL, a 29% and 43% increase compared to the virgin wood benchmark, respectively. Porosity and surface roughness values remained similar to the control. Inclusion of cellulose nanofibre and cationic starch additives further improved hand sheet properties. Overall, the integration of localised non-wood fibres into an uncoated paper substrate for flexible packaging applications offers potential economic and environmental benefits within India, without significant compromise to the physical properties of papers.
